etymology: American, recorded in the 1910s for a silly or stupid person, perhaps from older English dialect goff, a fool; the source is uncertain. By the 1940s and 50s goof also meant a blunder, and the verbs goof up (to bungle) and goof off (to loaf, to shirk) were everywhere, in the barracks and the schoolroom alike.
biblical_def: To a boy of 1952 a goof was either a mistake — dropping the fly ball, spilling the paint — or the silly kid who made one. "What a goof!" could be said with a laugh or a groan. Scripture is honest about goofs, because it is honest about people: "For in many things we offend all" (Jas 3:2). Every one of us drops the ball. The difference between a fool and a wise man is not that one never falls; it is what he does next. "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Pro 24:16). Small blunders are not the same as sins, and a grandfather should not treat a spilled glass of milk like a moral failure. But where a goof is a real wrong, the way back is wide open: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins" (1Jn 1:9). The other side of the word is goofing off, and there Scripture is plain: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise" (Pro 6:6). Laziness is not a goof; it is a habit. The best news for every goof-up is the faithfulness of God, whose mercies "are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness" (Lam 3:23). Christ did not come for people who never goof. He came for sinners, and He makes them new.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, from the 1910s; everywhere in the 1940s–50s) for a blunder or a silly person, with goof off for loafing — a word Scripture meets with honesty about falling and mercies new every morning (Lam 3:23).
webster_full: GOOF, n. (American slang, 1910s; common 1940s–50s) A blunder; a silly or foolish person. Also v., goof up (to bungle), goof off (to loaf). "I forgot the tickets — what a goof."
Decode for families: a goof is a mistake, and goofing off is loafing — the first can be forgiven with a laugh; the second needs fixing.
scriptures: Jas 3:2
For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.
For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Pro 6:6
Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise:
Lam 3:23
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
corruption_summary: A mostly gentle word for ordinary blunders; the cautions are against mocking people for their mistakes and against excusing laziness as mere goofing off.
corruption_paragraphs: Goof is one of the kinder words for a mistake. It assumes the blunder was silly rather than wicked, and often that is true. A family that can laugh at a goof, forgive it, and move on is practising grace in small things.

Two cautions. Calling a person a goof, over and over, can wound a child more than the parent knows, and Scripture forbids contempt for a brother (Mat 5:22). And goof off can make idleness sound harmless; the Bible does not treat it so (Pro 6:6). Keep the laugh for the spilled milk, and the correction for the chores left undone.
roots_summary: Dialect goff (a fool; uncertain) → American goof (1910s, a silly person) → 1940s–50s goof (a blunder), goof up, goof off.

etymology: American, of uncertain origin; first recorded in San Francisco around 1870 for the gangs of young toughs there, and the many stories told of its source remain unproven. By the 1940s and 50s it was the everyday word, often shortened to hood, for the leather-jacketed street tough and the juvenile delinquent of newspaper headlines.
biblical_def: In 1955 a hoodlum was the young tough on the corner — ducktail haircut, switchblade in his pocket, trouble in his eye — the kind of boy mothers warned their daughters about. Scripture knew the type three thousand years earlier. Solomon’s first counsel to his son is about the gang on the corner: "My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not" (Pro 1:10). The hoodlums say, come with us, there is easy money and excitement; the father answers, "My son, walk not thou in the way with them; refrain thy foot from their path" (Pro 1:15). "Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men" (Pro 4:14). The first psalm blesses the man who will not walk, stand, or sit with them (Psa 1:1). So a grandfather must be plain: stay away from the hoods. But Scripture will not let us stop there. Christ has a way of saving hoodlums. A thief crucified beside Him heard, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Luk 23:43). Paul wrote to a church full of former thieves and drunkards: "And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified" (1Co 6:11). The Christian keeps his children from the hoodlum’s path, and prays for the hoodlum, too.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, from San Francisco about 1870; an everyday 1940s–50s word) for a street tough — and Scripture both warns the young away from such company (Pro 1:10) and shows Christ saving such men (1Co 6:11).
webster_full: HOODLUM, n. (American, c. 1870; everyday 1940s–50s; short form hood) A young street tough; a ruffian; a petty criminal. "Stay away from that pool hall — it’s full of hoodlums."
Decode for families: a hoodlum is a street tough or a young criminal — a crowd to stay away from, and a person to pray for.
scriptures: Pro 1:10
My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not.
Pro 1:15
My son, walk not thou in the way with them; refrain thy foot from their path:
Pro 4:14
Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men.
And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.
corruption_summary: A plain word for a real danger; the only caution is that it can become a label that writes a young man off, when Christ has saved many hoodlums.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong in naming hoodlums for what they are. Violence, theft, and intimidation are sins, and Proverbs opens with a father warning his son against exactly this company. Parents of the 1950s who used the word were often right to worry.

The caution is in how the word is used. It was sometimes thrown at any boy with long sideburns or a poor family, and a label can harden a child into what he is called. Scripture judges by deeds, not haircuts, and it never treats any sinner as beyond reach (1Co 6:11). A Christian family can keep its children out of the gang and still hope and pray for the boys in it.

etymology: Jazz and beat slang of the 1950s, built on wig as slang for the head or mind (to flip one’s wig, to go crazy, is of the same family). Wig itself is short for periwig, the false hair of earlier centuries. To wig out was to lose control — to go wild with excitement or to go to pieces — and the phrase passed from the jazz clubs to the teenagers and on into the 1960s.
biblical_def: When a jazzman of 1957 said the crowd wigged out, he meant they went wild; when a mother said she was about to wig out, she meant the children had pushed her to the edge. Either way, the word means losing hold of the mind. Scripture prizes the opposite: "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind" (2Ti 1:7). Self-command is a kind of strength: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32), while the man who flies apart "is like a city that is broken down, and without walls" (Pro 25:28). There is real comfort here, because sometimes a person wigs out not from temper but from fear and strain, and God does not scold such a one so much as steady him: "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee" (Isa 26:3). The Gospels show the sharpest picture of all. A man so tormented by devils that no chain could hold him met Jesus, and afterward the townsfolk found him "sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind" (Mar 5:15). That is what Christ does for the wigged-out soul. A grandfather can tell the children: when you feel yourself coming apart, stop, pray, and fix your mind on the Lord who calms storms.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (jazz and beat talk, 1950s; from wig, the head or mind) for losing control — answered by the sound mind God gives (2Ti 1:7) and the tormented man Christ left sitting in his right mind (Mar 5:15).
webster_full: WIG OUT, v.i. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz and beat talk) To lose control; to go wild with excitement, or to go to pieces. "When the band hit that last chorus, the whole room wigged out."
Webster (1828) — WIG, noun 1. A covering for the head, consisting of hair interwoven or united by a kind of network; formerly much worn by men.
Decode for families: to wig out is to lose your head — and the 1828 wig was a covering of false hair, the very thing that flies off when you flip.
scriptures: For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
Isa 26:3
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
Mar 5:15
And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid.
corruption_summary: A lively word that can mean harmless excitement, but it can also make losing control sound fun or excusable, when Scripture calls us to a sound mind.
corruption_paragraphs: When wig out means only that the crowd went wild at a ballgame, it is harmless. Joy can be loud. And when a tired mother says she is about to wig out, she is confessing weakness, not boasting of it, and she deserves help more than a lecture.

The caution is that the jazz world of the 1950s sometimes used the word for the effects of drink and drugs, and the counterculture after it made wigging out a goal. Scripture never treats losing one’s mind as freedom. Rage, panic, and intoxication are things to be ruled, not sought (Pro 25:28). The Christian aims for the sound mind and the perfect peace God promises.
roots_summary: periwig → wig (false hair; later slang for the head or mind) → flip one’s wig → 1950s jazz slang wig out (to lose control).

usage: "Mom said if we tracked mud on her clean floor one more time, she’d wig out."
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind (2Ti 1:7).

etymology: From Old English col, moderately cold; by Webster’s day cool already meant calm and not excited as well as not hot, and to cool meant to allay passion. Cool it — calm down, stop, take it easy — is American slang recorded by the 1950s, at home both in jazz talk and on the playground, where it was the word for breaking up a quarrel before it became a fight.
biblical_def: "Cool it, you two!" was what a big brother said in 1956 when the twins started shoving over the last cookie. It means calm down, back off, stop before this gets worse — and it is wise counsel. Scripture says the same thing in older words: "The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with" (Pro 17:14). A quarrel is like a crack in a dam; the time to stop it is early. James gives the rule for a hot head: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19), "For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20). And Proverbs gives the tool: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (Pro 15:1). Not all anger is sin — "Be ye angry, and sin not" (Eph 4:26) — but most of ours is hasty and selfish, and it needs cooling. The one who says "cool it" at the right moment is doing the work of a peacemaker, and Jesus said, "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God" (Mat 5:9). The Prince of Peace made peace at the greatest cost, by the blood of His cross. A grandfather can teach the children to cool it with each other, and to be the one in the room who cools things down.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1950s) for calm down, stop, back off — from the 1828 cool, not excited by passion, and an echo of Solomon’s leave off contention, before it be meddled with (Pro 17:14).
webster_full: COOL IT, phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) Calm down; stop; take it easy. "Cool it, you two — Dad’s trying to sleep."

Webster (1828) — COOL, adjective 1. Moderately cold; being of a temperature between hot and cold; as cool air; cool water. 2. Not ardent or zealous; not angry; not fond; not excited by passion of any kind; indifferent; as a cool friend; a cool temper; a cool lover. COOL, verb transitive 2. To moderate excitement of temper; to allay, as passion of any kind; to calm, as anger; to abate, as love; to moderate, as desire, zeal or ardor; to render indifferent. COOL, verb intransitive 2. To lose the heat of excitement or passion; to become less ardent, angry, zealous, or affectionate; to become more moderate.
Decode for families: "cool it" means "calm down and stop" — good advice in any decade.
scriptures: The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with.
Jas 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
Jas 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
Mat 5:9
Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
corruption_summary: A wholesome phrase for making peace; the only cautions are that it can be said with contempt, or used to hush a wrong that ought to be heard.
corruption_paragraphs: Cool it is good counsel in two words, and Scripture says much the same. It belongs with the soft answer and the slow tongue. A family that uses it to stop squabbles is using slang for a godly end.

Two small cautions. Said with a sneer, "cool it" can be its own grievous word, stirring up the anger it means to calm (Pro 15:1). And sometimes it is used to silence a person with a real grievance; peacemaking means dealing with the wrong, not burying it. Cool the temper, then hear the complaint.
roots_summary: Old English col (moderately cold) → cool (calm, not excited by passion, 1828) → 1950s slang cool it (calm down, stop).

etymology: American, of unknown origin; recorded from about 1919 and common through the jazz age and the 1940s and 50s, spelled many ways (copasetic, copesetic). Sources in Hebrew, Italian, Louisiana French, and Chinook jargon have all been proposed, and none has been proved; the dictionaries still say origin unknown. It means entirely satisfactory, all in order.
biblical_def: When a mechanic in 1949 wiped his hands and said "Everything’s copacetic," he meant the engine was running right and there was nothing more to fix. It is a happy, slightly fancy word for all is well. Scripture has its own version. When the Shunammite woman’s son had died and she rode to the prophet, his servant was sent to ask her, "Is it well with thee? is it well with thy husband? is it well with the child? And she answered, It is well" (2Ki 4:26). She said it by faith, before the boy was raised. That is the Christian’s copacetic — not that nothing is wrong, but that God is working: "And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God" (Rom 8:28). Paul knew how to be full and how to be hungry and was content in both (Php 4:12). But Scripture also warns against a false all-is-well. The false prophets of Jeremiah’s day kept saying, "Peace, peace; when there is no peace" (Jer 6:14), and soothed the people while judgment came. The only truly copacetic state is peace with God, and that comes through Christ alone. At the beginning God looked on His work and "behold, it was very good" (Gen 1:31); at the end He will make all things new. Between those two, a grandfather can say "everything’s copacetic" with a smile, and mean the deeper thing: it is well with my soul.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, from about 1919, origin unknown; common through the 1950s) for entirely satisfactory, all in order — a word with a biblical twin in the Shunammite’s faith-filled It is well (2Ki 4:26).
webster_full: COPACETIC, adj. (American slang, c. 1919; common 1920s–50s; also copasetic) Entirely satisfactory; all in order; fine. "The car’s fixed, the bills are paid — everything’s copacetic."
Decode for families: copacetic means "everything’s fine" — nobody knows where the word came from, but everybody knew what it meant.
scriptures: Run now, I pray thee, to meet her, and say unto her, Is it well with thee? is it well with thy husband? is it well with the child? And she answered, It is well.
Rom 8:28
And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
Php 4:12
I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.
Jer 6:14
They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
Gen 1:31
And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.
corruption_summary: A cheerful, harmless word; its only danger is the false "all is well" that covers over trouble with God instead of facing it.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in copacetic. It is a fine word, a little showy, with a mystery for an origin, and it carries a contented spirit. Grandparents who said it were usually giving thanks without quite saying so.

The one caution is spiritual. A person can call his life copacetic while his soul is far from God, and the world is happy to agree. Jeremiah calls that healing the hurt slightly (Jer 6:14). True well-being begins with repentance and faith, and then a Christian can say "all is well" even in trouble, as the Shunammite did.

etymology: Gee is a softened form of the name Jesus, recorded in American English in the late nineteenth century; gee whiz (also gee whillikins) followed as a longer, playful form. By the 1940s and 50s it was the all-purpose exclamation of wholesome American youth, and gee-whiz even became an adjective for wide-eyed wonder. Few who said it knew whose name it trimmed.
biblical_def: "Gee whiz, Dad, can I borrow the car?" There was hardly a more innocent sentence in 1955. Grandparents who said gee whiz meant no harm at all, and most never knew that gee is a shortened form of the name of Jesus. That is exactly why the word is worth a quiet look. The third commandment says, "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain" (Exo 20:7). To take a name in vain is to use it emptily, as a noise. The name of Jesus is the highest name there is: God "hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name" (Php 2:9), "That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" (Php 2:10). Jesus Himself told His disciples, "Swear not at all" (Mat 5:34), and James repeats it: "let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay" (Jas 5:12). A softened form of a holy name is still a use of that name, and the Lord says "every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof" (Mat 12:36). None of this is a reason to scold Grandpa. It is a reason for a family to choose its exclamations with love for the name that saves — to say "wow" or "hot diggity" and keep the name of Jesus for prayer and praise.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American; gee a softened Jesus, late 19th c.) for a mild exclamation of surprise or wonder — innocently meant, but a minced oath that the third commandment invites us to examine (Exo 20:7).
webster_full: GEE WHIZ, interj. (American, late 19th c.; staple of the 1940s–50s; also gee, gee whillikins) A mild exclamation of surprise, wonder, or dismay. "Gee whiz, Mom, everybody else gets to go!"
Decode for families: gee is a shortened form of Jesus — Grandpa meant no harm, and we can honour him by choosing a different word.
scriptures: Exo 20:7
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
Php 2:9
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:
Php 2:10
That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth;
Mat 5:34
But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:
Jas 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
corruption_summary: An innocent-sounding exclamation that is, at its root, a softened use of the name of Jesus — a minced oath worth setting aside gently, without scorning those who meant no harm.
corruption_paragraphs: The grandparents who said gee whiz were not blaspheming in their hearts; they were using the clean slang of their day, and many chose it precisely to avoid swearing. Their instinct was good. That is why this needs saying gently and without any scorn for them.

Still, a minced oath borrows the sound of a holy name for an everyday noise, and Christ’s name is too precious for that (Php 2:9). The third commandment is not only about cursing; it is about using God’s name lightly. A Christian family can retire gee and gee whiz quietly, explain why to the children, and fill the gap with words that carry no name at all.

etymology: A softened form of God, recorded in English from the eighteenth century; like gosh and by golly, it let a speaker exclaim without saying the holy name outright. It was a favourite of 1940s and 50s America — "Golly, Pop!" — in schoolyards and farm kitchens alike.
biblical_def: "Golly, that’s a big fish!" In 1948 a boy on a dock might say it, and his grandmother might say "Good golly" when the pie burned. No one meant any harm; golly sounded about as wicked as a glass of milk. But the word began as a softened way of saying God, and that is worth knowing. When Jesus taught His disciples to pray, the very first request was about God’s name: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name" (Mat 6:9). To hallow is to treat as holy. The psalmist says, "holy and reverend is his name" (Psa 111:9). Moses told Israel to "fear this glorious and fearful name, THE LORD THY GOD" (Deu 28:58). And the third commandment is plain: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain" (Exo 20:7). A minced oath is a step back from the edge, and the people who used it were often trying to avoid swearing. That is to their credit. But the Christian can take one more step back. James says, "let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay" (Jas 5:12) — plain speech, with no oath and no echo of one. A grandfather who once said "golly" can teach his grandchildren why he now says "wow," and in doing so teach them to love the name above every name.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (English from the 18th c.; a 1940s–50s favourite) for a mild exclamation — a softened form of God, innocently meant, and a gentle occasion to learn what Hallowed be thy name asks of us (Mat 6:9).
webster_full: GOLLY, interj. (English, 18th c.; common in America 1940s–50s; also by golly, good golly) A mild exclamation of surprise or wonder. "Golly, Pop, look at the size of that trout!"
Decode for families: golly is a softened form of God — not a curse, but a word worth trading for one with no holy name in it.
scriptures: Mat 6:9
After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
He sent redemption unto his people: he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend is his name.
If thou wilt not observe to do all the words of this law that are written in this book, that thou mayest fear this glorious and fearful name, THE LORD THY GOD;
Exo 20:7
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
Jas 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
corruption_summary: A gentle-sounding exclamation that began as a softened use of the name of God; the grandparents meant no harm, and that is exactly why it is worth examining.
corruption_paragraphs: Golly is the mildest of words to modern ears, and those who said it were usually choosing it over something worse. That instinct honoured the third commandment in part, and no one should be scorned for it.

Yet the word still trades on the sound of God’s name, and Christ taught us to hallow that name before we ask for anything else (Mat 6:9). A family can let golly go without fuss, explain why, and keep God’s name for worship, prayer, and the solemn oath that is rightly taken.

Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name (Mat 6:9).

etymology: American, recorded from the late 1920s, a softened form of Jesus, often in the rhyming jeepers creepers (a minced form of Jesus Christ). The 1938 popular song "Jeepers Creepers" made the phrase a national catchword, and it stayed in the mouths of children through the 1940s and 50s.
biblical_def: "Jeepers!" said a girl in 1950 when a thunderclap shook the house; "Jeepers creepers!" said her brother when he saw the size of the dog next door. It is a funny, bouncy word, and those who said it meant nothing by it. But jeepers is a softened form of Jesus, and jeepers creepers trims Jesus Christ. That makes it worth a gentle second look, because no name in the world matters more. The angel told Joseph, "thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins" (Mat 1:21). Peter preached that "there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved" (Act 4:12). God has given Him "a name which is above every name" (Php 2:9). The third commandment guards that name: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain" (Exo 20:7). A minced oath is not the same as cursing, and a grandparent who said "jeepers" was not blaspheming. But a name that saves is too precious to become a startled noise, even a softened one. Paul shows the better use: "whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him" (Col 3:17). A family can let the old word go quietly and teach the children to speak the name of Jesus only with love.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, late 1920s; a 1938 popular song) for a mild exclamation — a softened Jesus (jeepers creepers for Jesus Christ), innocently meant, and a reminder of the name whereby we must be saved (Act 4:12).
webster_full: JEEPERS, interj. (American, late 1920s; also jeepers creepers) A mild exclamation of surprise or alarm. "Jeepers! That thunder about knocked me out of my chair."
Decode for families: jeepers is a softened Jesus — Grandma meant no harm, and we can keep that name for prayer.
scriptures: Mat 1:21
And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
Php 2:9
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:
Exo 20:7
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
Col 3:17
And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.
corruption_summary: A cheerful exclamation that is, at its root, a minced form of the name of Jesus Christ; meant innocently, it is still worth setting aside out of love for that name.
corruption_paragraphs: No one who said jeepers thought of it as an oath, and many chose it deliberately to keep from swearing. That instinct was right as far as it went, and the grandparents who said it deserve no scolding.

The Christian can go further. The name of Jesus is the name of salvation (Mat 1:21), and a word built from its sound is still a use of it. Jesus taught plain speech without oaths (Mat 5:37). Retiring jeepers is a small act of reverence, and explaining why is a good lesson for children about how much that name is worth.
roots_summary: Jesus, Jesus Christ → softened jeepers, jeepers creepers (late 1920s American) → 1938 popular song → 1940s–50s children’s exclamation.

Late 1920s American: jeepers, jeepers creepers — minced forms
1938: a popular song makes Jeepers Creepers a national catchword
1940s–50s: common children’s exclamation; kin to gee and gee whiz
usage: "Jeepers creepers, Billy, where’d you find a snake that big?"
Neither is there salvation in any other (Act 4:12).
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain (Exo 20:7).

etymology: American, recorded from the early twentieth century; of uncertain origin, it is generally taken as a softened substitute for stronger oaths built on holy. It became a favourite of radio baseball announcers and of boys in the stands, and was everywhere in the 1940s and 50s. The cow is there for the sound, not for any meaning.
biblical_def: "Holy cow, did you see that home run?" In 1951 a boy with his ear to the radio said it, and so did the man calling the game. It is a funny phrase, and there is nothing sacred about a cow. But the first word is holy, and that word belongs to God in a special way. The seraphim before His throne cry, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory" (Isa 6:3). God tells His people, "Be ye holy; for I am holy" (1Pe 1:16). The priests of Israel were charged to "put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean" (Lev 10:10). Holy cow grew up as a substitute for oaths that joined holy words to cheap exclamations, and it carries a faint echo of them. That makes it a minced oath of a mild kind, and the grandparents who used it meant no disrespect. Still, a Christian family can notice that the word holy is worth keeping for the things God has set apart: His name, His day, His Word, His people. "Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy hill; for the LORD our God is holy" (Psa 99:9). Save holy for Him, and cheer the home run some other way.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, early 20th c.; a 1940s–50s ballpark favourite) for a mild exclamation of surprise — a minced oath that spends the word holy on a cow, when Scripture keeps it for the LORD (Isa 6:3).
webster_full: HOLY COW, interj. (American, early 20th c.; common 1940s–50s) A mild exclamation of surprise or amazement. "Holy cow — that ball’s going all the way to the street!"
Decode for families: no one is calling a cow holy; it is a softened oath, and the word holy is worth saving for God.
scriptures: Isa 6:3
And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy.
And that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean;
Psa 99:9
Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy hill; for the LORD our God is holy.
Exo 20:7
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
corruption_summary: A comic, mild exclamation that stands in for stronger holy-oaths; harmless in intent, it still spends the word holy cheaply.
corruption_paragraphs: Holy cow is about as gentle as an exclamation can be, and it was usually chosen precisely because it was not swearing. The grandparents and ballpark announcers who said it were keeping their language clean by the standard of their day, and that should be honoured.

The Christian standard asks a little more. Scripture treats holiness as God’s own glory and calls His people to keep a difference between holy and common (Lev 10:10). When holy becomes a sound effect, the word grows thin. Letting the phrase go is a small way to teach children that holy is a great word, and that the third commandment (Exo 20:7) reaches to the edges of our speech.
roots_summary: holy (Old English halig, set apart, sacred) → stronger holy-oaths → softened holy cow (early 20th c. American) → 1940s–50s ballpark favourite.
roots_lines: Old English halig — holy, sacred, set apart
Older exclamations joining holy words to oaths
Early 20th c. American: holy cow — a softened substitute
1940s–50s: favourite of radio baseball announcers and their listeners
Kindred forms: holy mackerel, holy smoke
usage: "Holy cow, Grandpa, the river’s right up to the porch!"
Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory (Isa 6:3).
Be ye holy; for I am holy (1Pe 1:16).

etymology: American in its sense of a claim ("dibs on the front seat"), recorded in the 1930s; probably from the older children’s game dibstones, a form of jacks played with small stones or knucklebones, whose name was shortened to dibs. By the 1940s and 50s every American child knew that calling dibs settled who got the window seat, the last drumstick, or the first turn.
biblical_def: In 1950, with five children piling into a Chevy, the loudest one hollered "Dibs on the window!" and the matter was settled. Calling dibs is a child’s law of first claim, and it is often fair enough. But Scripture tells a story that turns dibs on its head. When Abram’s herdsmen and Lot’s were quarrelling, Abram, the elder, gave the younger man first choice: "if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right" (Gen 13:9). And "Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan" (Gen 13:11) — he called dibs on the best land, and it led him toward Sodom. The mother of James and John called dibs for her boys on the best seats in the kingdom (Mat 20:21), and Jesus answered that greatness is service. He told His hearers to take the lowest room at a feast, "that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher" (Luk 14:10). Paul gives the rule: "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves" (Php 2:3), and "in honour preferring one another" (Rom 12:10). Christ Himself did not grasp at His rights but took the form of a servant. A grandfather can let the children call dibs — and then teach them the joy of giving the window seat away.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1930s; probably from the children’s game dibstones) for a claim on something ("dibs on the front seat") — a word Scripture turns around with in honour preferring one another (Rom 12:10).
webster_full: DIBS, n. pl. (American slang, 1930s; children’s staple 1940s–50s) A claim to something, staked by calling it first. "Dibs on the front seat!"
Decode for families: calling dibs means "I claim it" — and giving up your dibs is one of the first lessons in Christian kindness.
scriptures: Gen 13:9

Is not the whole land before thee? separate thyself, I pray thee, from me: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left.
Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan; and Lot journeyed east: and they separated themselves the one from the other.

But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee.
Php 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;
corruption_summary: A harmless children’s custom for settling who goes first; the only caution is the grabbing spirit it can train, which Scripture answers with preferring others.
corruption_paragraphs: Dibs is a rough-and-ready kind of fairness, and families have used it for generations to end arguments quickly. There is nothing wicked in it; first come, first served is a reasonable rule for window seats.

But children learn habits through games. A child who always races to call dibs is practising looking out for number one, and Lot’s choice shows where that can lead (Gen 13:11). Scripture asks for the reverse habit: look on the things of others (Php 2:4). Parents can honour a fair dibs and still praise the child who gives his away.
roots_summary: dibstones (children’s game of jacks) → dibs → 1930s American slang (a claim) → 1940s–50s children’s law of first claim.
roots_lines: dibstones — an old children’s game of jacks with stones or knucklebones
Shortened to dibs
1930s American slang: dibs — a claim to something
1940s–50s: "dibs on the window," "first dibs"
usage: "I called dibs on the front seat, then let Grandma have it — she smiled the whole way to church."
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory (Php 2:3).
Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another (Rom 12:10).

etymology: English, of uncertain origin, recorded from the late eighteenth century (spelled fogy or fogey) for an old man, especially one behind the times. Old fogey was a common teasing name in the 1940s and 50s for a parent or teacher who did not understand the new music, the new slang, or the new cars.
biblical_def: To a teenager of 1957, anyone who did not like rock and roll was an old fogey — the principal, the pastor, Dad. Now those teenagers are the grandparents, and the word has come back around. Scripture has a great deal of respect for old people, and it does not allow the young to sneer at them. "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD" (Lev 19:32). Gray hair is not a mark of being behind the times: "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" (Pro 16:31). The old have something the young do not: "With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding" (Job 12:12). And sometimes the old ways are the right ones: "ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls" (Jer 6:16). Scripture is not sentimental, though. Not every old custom is godly; Jesus rebuked men who held "the tradition of men" above the commandment of God (Mar 7:8). The test is not old or new but true or false. A grandfather can laugh at being called an old fogey, and then tell his grandchildren that the oldest thing he knows — the gospel of Christ — is also the newest, for it makes all things new.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (English from the late 18th c.; a 1940s–50s teen tease) for an old-fashioned person — a word Scripture answers with honour the face of the old man (Lev 19:32), while testing every custom, old or new, by God’s Word.
webster_full: FOGEY, n. (English, late 18th c.; common in America 1940s–50s, usually old fogey) An old-fashioned person; one behind the times. "Dad’s such an old fogey — he still calls the radio the wireless."
Decode for families: an old fogey is someone behind the times — and the Bible says to honour him anyway, and often to listen.
scriptures: Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.
With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Mar 7:8
For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do.
corruption_summary: A teasing word that is often affectionate, but at its worst it trains the young in contempt for the old, which Scripture forbids.
corruption_paragraphs: Many grandparents wear old fogey as a badge and laugh at it, and in that spirit there is little harm. Every generation teases the one before, and a family with good humour can enjoy the joke.

The trouble comes when the joke becomes a habit of contempt. A culture that calls its elders fogeys stops asking them anything, and Scripture calls that foolish (Job 12:12). Peter tells the younger to submit to the elder and all to be clothed with humility (1Pe 5:5). Children can be taught to tease kindly and to listen closely.
roots_summary: Of uncertain origin → English fogy, fogey (late 18th c., an old man behind the times) → old fogey → 1940s–50s teen tease.
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; perhaps related to foggy (dull, flabby)
Late 18th c. English: fogy, fogey — an old man; one behind the times
19th–20th c.: old fogey — the standard form
1940s–50s: teen name for parents and teachers; kin to square
usage: "Call me an old fogey if you like, but a man ought to take his hat off indoors."
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness (Pro 16:31).
With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding (Job 12:12).

etymology: From Hick, a familiar form of the name Richard, used in English from the sixteenth century as a generic name for a country fellow (as Hob and Hodge were). American English kept it, and in the 1940s and 50s hick and hick town were the city boy’s names for the farm boy and his home.
biblical_def: When a city kid of 1949 called somebody a hick, he meant a farm boy with hay in his hair, who talked slow and did not know how to work a jukebox. It was a put-down, and a strange one, because God has always done His best work among hicks. When Philip told Nathanael that the Messiah came from a backwater town, Nathanael said what every city man thinks: "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" (Joh 1:46). Philip’s answer is the right one to every sneer: "Come and see." The prophet Amos was a country man and said so: "I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit" (Amo 7:14). The first men to hear of Christ’s birth were "shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night" (Luk 2:8). The apostles were fishermen whom the city rulers took for unlearned men. Paul explains it: "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27). So James will not let the church look down on anyone: "have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons" (Jas 2:1). A grandfather who grew up on a farm can tell his grandchildren the truth: the Lord Jesus came from a hick town, and He was not ashamed of it.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (from Hick, a pet form of Richard, used for a rustic since the 16th c.) for a country bumpkin — a sneer Scripture answers with a Saviour from despised Nazareth (Joh 1:46) and shepherds as the first to hear of His birth.
webster_full: HICK, n. (English from the 16th c.; common American slang 1940s–50s; also hick town) A country bumpkin; an unsophisticated rural person. "He’s just a hick from out past the grain elevator."
Decode for families: a hick is a country person, and the word is usually a put-down — but Jesus grew up in a hick town.
scriptures: Joh 1:46
And Nathanael said unto him, Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? Philip saith unto him, Come and see.
Amo 7:14
Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:
Luk 2:8
And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
Jas 2:1
My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.
corruption_summary: A contemptuous word for country people; it carries the pride of the city over the farm, which Scripture overturns again and again.
corruption_paragraphs: Hick is not a curse, and many country people use it of themselves with a grin. But in the mouth of an outsider it is contempt, a way of saying that plain, rural, unfashionable people count for less. Scripture calls that respect of persons, and forbids it (Jas 2:1).

The cure is to look at whom God chooses. Shepherds, herdsmen, fishermen, and a carpenter from Nazareth carry the story of redemption (1Co 1:27). A Christian family can teach its children to admire the farmer’s skill, to welcome the newcomer with the slow drawl, and to remember that the Lord of glory was called a Nazarene.
roots_summary: Richard → pet form Hick → 16th c. English generic name for a country fellow → American hick, hick town → 1940s–50s city slang.

Kindred generic names: Hob, Hodge; later American rube
1940s–50s American slang: hick, hick town — a rustic; a small town
usage: "They called Grandpa a hick when he came to the city, till they saw him fix the plant’s broken boiler in an hour."
